resources.string: Your body clock is on %1$s time.
To adapt: %1$s with your plan, %2$s without one.
Chart of hours your body clock is off %1$s time. With your plan: %2$s at landing, in sync in %3$s. Without a plan, as a rough guide: %4$s at landing, %5$s.

%1$s is %2$s ahead, but this plan moves your body clock %3$s later instead. After a big jump east, the destination\'s morning light falls before your body\'s low point, where light pushes the clock the wrong way. Most body clocks also run a little longer than 24 hours, so moving later each day comes more easily. Experts still disagree on where the cut-off lies.

%1$s is %2$s behind, but this plan moves your body clock %3$s earlier instead. That\'s further round the clock face, but for this trip it\'s the direction the plan\'s light and sleep timing can push your body clock most reliably. Experts still disagree on where the cut-off lies.
Adapting starts with your first pre-trip day.
No jet lag expected. Enjoy the trip.
%1$s and %2$s keep nearly the same hours. Keep your usual sleep, %3$s to %4$s local time, and get some daylight in the morning.
Short trip: staying on home time
You\'re back before your body could settle, so the plan keeps your clock on %1$s time. Sleep on home hours where you can, and use light to stay sharp.
Nothing to do yet. First up: %1$s, %2$s at %3$s.
You landed on %1$s time. Safe travels home.
Not medical advice. Healthy adults only; not for flight crew on duty.
One missed block is fine: adapting just takes a little longer. Pick it back up at the next one.
Not medical advice. If you have a health condition, are pregnant or take medication, talk to a doctor before changing your sleep or using melatonin.
Nothing is scheduled right now, so there\'s nothing to explain. Enjoy it.
Light now lands just after your body clock\'s low point, which nudges the clock earlier. That\'s exactly the direction you need to go.
Light now lands just before your body clock\'s low point, which nudges the clock later. That\'s exactly the direction you need to go.
Light now would push your body clock the wrong way and undo some progress. A little darkness here protects the shift.
A small dose of melatonin in the afternoon or evening tells your body night is coming sooner, which moves the clock earlier.
Melatonin in the morning nudges your clock later. Keep the dose small.
This sleep is timed to your shifting body clock, halfway between your old schedule and the new one. Meeting it in the middle makes the move smoother.
Sleeping during your destination\'s night anchors your body clock to local time.
Your trip is short, so the plan keeps your body clock on home time instead of moving it twice.
Caffeine helps you stay sharp now and wears off before your next sleep.
Caffeine lingers for hours. Skipping it now protects your next sleep.
This is your body clock\'s low point while you\'re awake: reactions slow down and focus drifts. Avoid driving if you can.
A short nap takes the edge off without anchoring you to the old time zone. Keep it short so tonight\'s sleep stays deep.
Your flight. The cards around it make the time in the air work for you.
It\'s night for your body. If you can\'t sleep on planes, rest in the dark with an eye mask: darkness still helps the shift.
Go outside if you can; even a cloudy sky beats indoor light. No sunglasses. Stuck indoors? Sit by a window with every light on.
Avoid dim rooms. Ordinary daylight or bright indoor light is enough. No sunglasses.
Dark sunglasses on, even indoors, even if it feels silly. Especially if it feels silly. Dim your screens and keep away from windows.
Cool, dark and quiet. An eye mask and earplugs help. If you can\'t sleep, just stay in the dark.
Set an alarm. A short nap refreshes; a long one steals from tonight.
Only if you\'re tired. Keep it short and set an alarm.
Take the type and dose you\'ve agreed with your doctor. Don\'t drive for a few hours afterwards.
Little and often: a small coffee or tea every couple of hours works better than one big cup.
Switch to water, herbal tea or decaf until your next sleep.
Take it easy. Avoid driving and big decisions if you can; a short walk helps.
Follow the cards that run during the flight: they say when to sleep and when to keep the window shade up.
Based on the human phase response curve to light (Khalsa et al. 2003; St Hilaire et al. 2012).
Light on the wrong side of the phase response curve moves the clock the wrong way (Khalsa et al. 2003).
Based on the phase response curve to melatonin (Burgess et al. 2010).
Shifting sleep gradually around travel speeds up adaptation (Eastman & Burgess 2009).
For trips of a few days, staying on home time avoids two rounds of jet lag (Waterhouse et al. 2007).
Caffeine\'s half-life is 3–5 hours; caffeine even 6 hours before bed shortens sleep (Drake et al. 2013).
Alertness bottoms out near the body temperature minimum (Dijk & Czeisler 1995).
Short naps relieve sleep pressure with little effect on the body clock (Lovato & Lack 2010).
Times come from your flight details, in each airport\'s local time.
Darkness at the right time protects the shift even without sleep (Eastman & Burgess 2009).
